description: WHEN ONE DOOR CLOSES, ANOTHER OPENS
summary: Abandoned But Not Forgotten is an interactive educational website built by Team Crop for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge. It turns NASA’s retired Moon and Mars hardware into stories for school-age learners. Students can explore ten verified missions, including Apollo 11’s Eagle, the Lunar Roving Vehicles, Viking, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Phoenix, and InSight. Each mission page explains what the machine was built to do, what it discovered, how it ended, and links to NASA sources. The site also offers a timeline, comparison tool, quiz, Mission Detective game, and a mission builder. Its core message: abandoned does not mean forgotten, because the discoveries continue.
details:
Abandoned But Not Forgotten is an interactive web archive of NASA’s retired Moon and Mars hardware, designed for school-age learners. Students can browse ten NASA missions, including Apollo 11’s Eagle lander, the Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicles, Surveyor 3, Viking, Pathfinder and Sojourner, Mars Polar Lander, Spirit, Opportunity, Phoenix, and InSight. They can filter by planet, hardware type, era, and status, or search by keyword.

Each mission page tells a complete story: what the machine was built to do, its journey, how it works (power, communication, science, mobility), what it discovered and why that mattered, how its mission ended, and where it is now. Every page lists clickable NASA and NASA/JPL sources.

Students can also explore a timeline, compare any two missions side by side, take a 10-question quiz, play Mission Detective (guess the mission from clues), and design a fictional mission in a simulator clearly labeled as not a real NASA mission. All content loads from local JSON files, so the site works with no backend and no API keys.

What benefits does it have?

It makes scattered technical history easy to understand. Technical terms are explained in plain language, and statuses (mission complete, inactive, lost) are shown clearly without sensationalizing failures. Because the content is sourced, teachers and parents can trust it and students can check the original NASA pages. It is mobile responsive, keyboard accessible, and respects reduced-motion settings.

What is the intended impact?

We want students to see that a machine going silent is not the end of its story. Its data, discoveries, and engineering lessons keep shaping later missions. We hope this inspires curiosity about space exploration and shows young people how engineering, science, and discovery connect.

What tools, languages, and software did you use?

HTML5, CSS3, and vanilla JavaScript, with JSON data files. We used Git and GitHub for version control and GitHub Pages for hosting, and a local Python web server for testing. Mission facts were researched from NASA, NASA/JPL, NASA Science, and NASA Goddard sources. We used an AI assistant (Claude) to help plan, research, and generate code. (Space Apps asks teams to disclose AI use, so keep this line.) No special hardware was required.

How is it creative?

It treats abandoned hardware as characters with life stories, using an anatomy explorer, a journey timeline, and games rather than a static list of facts. The central “Machine → Data → Discovery → Knowledge → Future Exploration” flow reframes “abandoned” as a legacy. A NASA-inspired deep-space design makes it feel like a digital museum.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Accuracy: we linked every fact to a source and labeled anything unverifiable as unknown rather than guessing.
  • Audience: simple language, short sections, and playful activities for young learners.
  • Reliability: no backend or API dependency, so it works offline and during live judging.
  • Accessibility and mobile use: semantic HTML, visible focus states, and responsive layouts.
  • Scope: ten well-sourced missions instead of many shallow ones.

Current limitations: the illustrations are simple SVG drawings rather than NASA photos. A planetary map, story mode, and AI archivist are planned future improvements.
